text: You open a text editor, press the letter E, and it appears instantly. It feels like the simplest, most fundamental thing a computer can do. But under the hood, translating that keystroke into the shape you see on your monitor is a mathematical nightmare. Drawing a rectangle is easy. You tell the GPU to fill a block of pixels with a color. But drawing text is arguably one of the most complex, computationally expensive tasks your operating system handles. Today, we're going to look at why making text readable is a fight against math, physics, and human biology. The root of the problem is that fonts are not pictures. If a font were just a collection of pixels, it would get horribly pixelated and blurry the moment you zoomed in or increased the font size. To be infinitely scalable, fonts are built using mathematical formulas. Specifically, they are constructed from vector graphics relying heavily on Bézier curves. When you download a font file, you aren't downloading images of letters. You are downloading a set of mathematical instructions. The file simply says, "Start at this exact coordinate, curve towards this control point, and end here." But here is where the nightmare begins. This math represents infinite continuous precision, but your screen is not continuous. Your screen is a rigid, discrete grid of square pixels. The fundamental problem of text rendering is taking a perfectly smooth mathematical curve and forcing it onto a low-resolution grid of squares. This translation process is called rasterization. When you try to map a curve onto a pixel grid, you inevitably get jagged edges. We call this the staircase effect or aliasing. To fix this, engineers use anti-aliasing. Instead of a pixel being purely black or purely white, the rendering engine calculates the coverage of the mathematical curve over a specific pixel. If the curve only covers half the pixel, the engine colors it fifty percent gray.
